result:
The first time the town’s clocks disagreed, nobody thought much of it.

The bakery opened seven minutes early. The school bell rang during a sentence about volcanoes. At the station, a man missed a train that, according to the clock above his head, had not yet arrived.

By Thursday, the discrepancies had become personal.

The clock in the florist’s shop ran quickly whenever someone bought roses out of guilt. The courthouse clock stopped for anyone waiting to hear a verdict. In the kitchen of a woman whose son lived overseas, the second hand hesitated each time the telephone rang.

A clockmaker was summoned.

He was old enough to remember when the town had wanted a fountain and had settled, after considerable debate, for a second bench. He visited every clock with a leather bag of tools. He listened. He tightened screws. He declined coffee in twelve separate buildings.

“Well?” the mayor asked.

“The clocks are fine,” he said.

This was considered an unhelpful diagnosis.

That evening, the clockmaker took down the clock above his own workbench. Behind it was a pale circle where the wallpaper had not faded. He stood looking at this for a long while.

Then he called his brother, with whom he had not spoken in nineteen years.

They discussed the weather first.

There was quite a lot of weather to get through.

In the morning, the bakery opened seven minutes early again. The baker had stopped trying to correct the clock; he simply came downstairs when he heard the delivery van.

Across town, the clockmaker’s telephone rang while he was making breakfast.

“Forgot to ask,” his brother said. “Do you still have Dad’s ladder?”

The clockmaker put down his knife.

“You can’t possibly want that back.”

“No,” his brother said. “I need to borrow it.”
